Occam’s Razor is Only as Sharp as Your ELBO

 

Ethan Harvey          Michael C. Hughes

Tufts University ethan.harvey@tufts.edu          Tufts University michael.hughes@tufts.edu

Abstract

The marginal likelihood, also known as the evidence, is regarded as a mathematical embodiment of Occam’s razor, enabling model selection that avoids overfitting. The evidence lower bound (ELBO) objective from variational inference has also been used for similar purposes. Prior work has shown that restricting the approximate posterior family via a mean-field approximation can lead the ELBO to underfit. In this paper, we show how ELBO-based hyperparameter learning in a simple over-parameterized regression model can also produce overfitting, depending on the assumed rank of the covariance matrix in a Gaussian approximate posterior. Surprisingly, among only the underfit and overfit options, Bayesian model selection via the evidence itself sometimes prefers the overfit version, while the ELBO does not. Bayesian practitioners hoping to scale to large models should be cautious about how reduced-rank assumptions needed for tractability may impact the potential for model selection.

1 INTRODUCTION

Bayesian model selection relies on the marginal likelihood, commonly referred to as the evidence, to quantify how well a model explains the observed data while accounting for model complexity. The evidence is regarded as a mathematical embodiment of Occam’s razor, favoring simpler models that explain the data well (Jeffreys, 1939; MacKay, 1991; Rasmussen and Ghahramani, 2000; Grünwald, 2005). Yet modern practitioners face barriers to using the evidence directly for training or model selection with prediction models based on deep neural networks (DNNs). Even computing the marginal likelihood exactly is intractable for typical DNN-based prediction models. This difficulty has led to the adoption of variational inference (VI) as a scalable approximate inference technique for Bayesian deep learning.

††footnotetext: Code: github.com/ethanharvey98/overfitting-ELBO

Given a joint model over hidden weights ww and observed labels yy, VI approximates the true posterior p⁡(w∣y)p(w\mid y) with a simpler distribution q⁡(w)q(w), adjusting the parameters defining q⁡(w)q(w) to solve an optimization problem. The objective function to maximize is a tractable lower bound on the log-evidence, known as the evidence lower bound (ELBO; Jordan et al., 1999; Blei et al., 2017). The ELBO is often described as giving rise to Occam’s razor (Hinton and Van Camp, 1993; Barber and Bishop, 1998b; Barber and Bishop, 1998a). Past work has used the ELBO for model selection in mixture models (Ueda and Ghahramani, 2002; McGrory and Titterington, 2007), Gaussian processes (GPs; Titsias, 2009; Damianou and Lawrence, 2013; Hensman et al., 2015; Lalchand et al., 2022), and DNNs (KC et al., 2021).

However, ELBO-based learning may not always provide an Occam’s razor-like benefit for model selection. The tightness of the bound linking the ELBO to the ideal evidence depends on the chosen density family for q⁡(w)q(w). Prior work has shown that mean-field VI can lead to underfitting (Coker et al., 2022; Harvey et al., 2024; Harvey et al., 2026). Yet to our knowledge an example of ELBO-based overfitting has not been demonstrated.

In this short paper, we provide a clear case of ELBO-based overfitting. The case arises in an over-parameterized Bayesian linear regression model where the posterior over weights is approximated by a Gaussian q⁡(w)q(w). Using a rank-deficient, specifically rank-1, parameterization of the covariance matrix leads to over overfitting. In this case, the ELBO degenerates to a maximum a posteriori (MAP)-like objective which leads to a systematic underestimate of the likelihood variance (Bishop and Qazaz, 1996). In contrast, a diagonal covariance matrix corresponding to the independence assumptions underlying mean-field VI recovers the better known case of underfitting.

Scrutinizing rank-1 covariance assumptions matters because such approximations have been recently proposed for efficient and scalable Bayesian neural networks (BNNs; Dusenberry et al., 2020). For some big models, diagonal or low-rank approximations may be the only affordable option. Yet our work suggests the ELBO is not always suitability for model selection or hyperparameter learning in such cases.

2 BACKGROUND: REGRESSION

We have a training set {(xi,yi)}i=1N\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N} where xi∈ℝDx_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} denotes an input vector and yi∈ℝy_{i}\in\mathbb{R} denotes a scalar output or target. Let ϕ⁡(⋅):ℝD→ℝR\phi(\cdot):\mathbb{R}^{D}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{R} be a feature map that defines the design matrix Φ=[ϕ​(x1)⊤;…;ϕ​(xN)⊤]∈ℝN×R\Phi=[\phi(x_{1})^{\top};\dots;\phi(x_{N})^{\top}]\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times R} and y=[y1;…;yN]∈ℝNy=[y_{1};\dots;y_{N}]\in\mathbb{R}^{N} denote the target vector.

Prior and Likelihood. We assume a Bayesian linear regression model with parameter vector w∈ℝRw\in\mathbb{R}^{R}. The prior over parameters is a zero-mean Gaussian,

pη​(w)=𝒩⁡(w∣0R,Σp)\displaystyle p_{\eta}(w)=\mathcal{N}(w\mid 0_{R},\Sigma_{p}) (1)

where 0R0_{R} denotes the RR-dimensional zero vector and Σp\Sigma_{p} is an R×RR\times R covariance matrix. Conditioned on the parameter vector ww, the observations are generated according to a Gaussian likelihood,

pη​(y∣w)=𝒩⁡(y∣Φ​w,σy2​IN)\displaystyle p_{\eta}(y\mid w)=\mathcal{N}(y\mid\Phi w,\sigma_{y}^{2}I_{N}) (2)

where σy2\sigma_{y}^{2} denotes the observation noise variance.

Let vector η\eta denote the hyperparameters that control under or overfitting. These could include σy\sigma_{y} as well as scalars that control the prior variance in Σp\Sigma_{p} or the feature map ϕ⁡(⋅)\phi(\cdot).

Posterior. Due to conjugacy, the true posterior distribution over ww is also Gaussian. We have

pη​(w∣y)=𝒩⁡(w∣μ∗,Σ∗),\displaystyle p_{\eta}(w\mid y)=\mathcal{N}(w\mid\mu^{*},\Sigma^{*}), (3)

with μ∗=1σy2​Σ∗​Φ⊤​y\mu^{*}=\tfrac{1}{\sigma_{y}^{2}}\Sigma^{*}\Phi^{\top}y and Σ∗=(Σp−1+1σy2​Φ⊤​Φ)−1\Sigma^{*}=(\Sigma_{p}^{-1}+\tfrac{1}{\sigma_{y}^{2}}\Phi^{\top}\Phi)^{-1}.

Marginal Likelihood. Again due to the compositional properties of the Gaussian, marginalizing over ww yields the marginal of yy

pη​(y)=𝒩⁡(y∣0N,σy2​IN+Φ​Σp​Φ⊤).\displaystyle p_{\eta}(y)=\mathcal{N}(y\mid 0_{N},\sigma_{y}^{2}I_{N}+\Phi\Sigma_{p}\Phi^{\top}). (4)

The subscript η\eta here reminds us that this depends on the hyperparameters defined above. We can estimate the value of η\eta by maximizing the marginal likelihood given the training set, known as type-II maximum likelihood estimation. Estimating η\eta in this way naturally encodes an Occam’s razor preference for the simplest well-fit model even when R>NR>N, while directly maximizing pη​(w,y)p_{\eta}(w,y) usually severely overfits.

Approximate Posterior. VI approximates the true (intractable) posterior p⁡(w∣y)p(w\mid y) with a simpler distribution q⁡(w)q(w). We assume q⁡(w)q(w) is Gaussian, q⁡(w)=𝒩⁡(w∣μq,Σq)q(w)=\mathcal{N}(w\mid\mu_{q},\Sigma_{q}). We later explore different versions of the parametric form of the covariance matrix Σq\Sigma_{q}, such as diagonal or rank-1.

Evidence Lower Bound. The ELBO objective (Jordan et al., 1999; Blei et al., 2017), is a function of μq,Σq,\mu_{q},\Sigma_{q}, and hyperparameters η\eta, defined as J⁡(μq,Σq,η):=J(\mu_{q},\Sigma_{q},\eta):=

𝔼q⁡(w)[logpη(y∣w)]−DKL(q(w)∥pη(w)).\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{q(w)}\left[\log p_{\eta}(y\mid w)\right]-D_{\text{KL}}\left(q(w)\parallel p_{\eta}(w)\right). (5)

A bound relation holds: J⁡(μq,Σq,η)≤log⁡pη​(y)J(\mu_{q},\Sigma_{q},\eta)\leq\log p_{\eta}(y).

We fit the model to data by finding specific values of μq,Σq,η\mu_{q},\Sigma_{q},\eta that maximize JJ. For our chosen regression model with a Gaussian approximate posterior qq, we can compute the ELBO in closed-form (see App. A). We maximize it using distinct updates to μq,Σq,\mu_{q},\Sigma_{q}, and η\eta that interleave closed-form updates and gradient steps.

3 OVERFITTING EXAMPLE

For simplicity, throughout this section we assume the prior covariance is the R×RR\times R identity matrix Σp=IR\Sigma_{p}=I_{R}.

Rank-1 Covariance. Consider restricting q⁡(w)q(w) to a rank-1 covariance matrix,

q⁡(w)=𝒩⁡(μq,vq​vq⊤+ε​IR),\displaystyle q(w)=\mathcal{N}(\mu_{q},v_{q}v_{q}^{\top}+\varepsilon I_{R}), (6)

where vq∈ℝRv_{q}\in\mathbb{R}^{R} is a learnable single direction of uncertainty and ε​IR\varepsilon I_{R} is a fixed small diagonal component added to keep the covariance positive definite.

While this covariance models uncertainty along a single direction vqv_{q}, we will show it can lead to overfitting when the number of parameters is greater than the number of data points R>NR>N.

Optimizing the ELBO leads to a null-space collapse. Consider optimizing the ELBO JJ with respect to vqv_{q}, the direction of uncertainty in the rank-1 covariance. The gradient here is

∂J∂vq=−1σy2​Φ⊤​Φ​vq−vq+1‖vq‖22+ε​vq.\displaystyle\frac{\partial J}{\partial v_{q}}=-\frac{1}{\sigma_{y}^{2}}\Phi^{\top}\Phi v_{q}-v_{q}+\frac{1}{\|v_{q}\|_{2}^{2}+\varepsilon}v_{q}. (7)

In our over-parameterized setting with R>NR>N, we know there are infinitely many non-zero vectors vqv_{q} in the null space of Φ\Phi. We seek optima of JJ in this null space by setting ∂J∂vq=0\frac{\partial J}{\partial v_{q}}=0, and find as a solution any vector that simultaneously satisfies ‖vq‖22=1−ε\|v_{q}\|_{2}^{2}=1-\varepsilon, Φ​vq=0\Phi v_{q}=0, and vq≠0v_{q}\neq 0. This implies that the model constructs uncertainty orthogonal to the features Φ\Phi to maximize the entropy of q⁡(w)q(w) without incurring a likelihood cost.

Under this condition, the ELBO simplifies significantly. With the entropy term maximized independently of the data or prior terms, the objective for the mean parameters μq\mu_{q} degenerates to a MAP-like objective, J⁡(μq,…,η):=const+J(\mu_{q},\dots,\eta):=\text{const}+\phantom{text}

−12​[N​log⁡(2​π​σy2)+1σy2​‖y−Φ​μq‖22+‖μq‖22].\displaystyle-\frac{1}{2}\left[N\log(2\pi\sigma_{y}^{2})+\frac{1}{\sigma_{y}^{2}}\|y-\Phi\mu_{q}\|_{2}^{2}+\|\mu_{q}\|_{2}^{2}\right]. (8)

Because the model has the capacity to interpolate the training data (R>NR>N), there exist parameters μq\mu_{q} such that the training error (middle term above) is effectively zero regardless of σy\sigma_{y}. As a result, the objective function with respect to the hyperparameters η\eta becomes dominated by the log-determinant (first term above), which drives σy→0\sigma_{y}\rightarrow 0, as discussed in Bishop and Qazaz (1996).

Despite using a variational framework intended to capture uncertainty, the simplified rank-1 covariance structure in q⁡(w)q(w) allows the model to bypass the Occam’s razor penalty. The result is a systematic underestimate of the likelihood variance σy2\sigma_{y}^{2} and clear overfitting, which we confirm with experiments below.

4 EXPERIMENTS

To empirically validate how q⁡(w)q(w) choices may lead to overfitting, we implement the regression model and VI framework above to estimate both μq,Σq\mu_{q},\Sigma_{q} and hyperparameters η\eta by ELBO maximization.

We focus on a synthetic dataset, formed by sampling inputs from the standard univariate normal distribution x∼𝒩⁡(0,1)x\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1) and outputs from a noisy sinusoidal function y=sin⁡(3​x)+εy=\sin(3x)+\varepsilon where ε∼𝒩⁡(0,0.01)\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,0.01).

We use random Fourier features (RFFs; Rahimi and Recht, 2007) for the feature map ϕ⁡(⋅)\phi(\cdot) (defined in App. B). We select the number of features RR, and the feature map ϕ⁡(⋅)\phi(\cdot) produces an RR-dimensional vector for each xix_{i} that approximates a radial basis function (RBF) kernel, ϕ​(xi)⊤​Σp​ϕ​(xj)≈σk2​exp⁡(−12​‖xi−xj‖22ℓk2)\phi(x_{i})^{\top}\Sigma_{p}\phi(x_{j})\approx\sigma_{k}^{2}\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\frac{\|x_{i}-x_{j}\|_{2}^{2}}{\ell_{k}^{2}}\right) when Σp=IR\Sigma_{p}=I_{R}. This approximation is increasingly accurate as R→∞R\rightarrow\infty.

The complete set of hyperparameters for this model are the likelihood standard deviation σy\sigma_{y}, kernel lengthscale ℓk\ell_{k}, and kernel outputscale σk\sigma_{k}. We train parameters and hyperparameters with coordinate ascent if there exists closed-form updates and gradient ascent otherwise. For gradient ascent, we use ADAM (Kingma and Ba, 2015) with a cosine annealing learning rate and grid search over several initial learning rates {0.1, 0.01, 0.001, 0.0001}.

5 RESULTS

Fig. 1 shows the predictive posterior for a Gaussian approximate posterior with a diagonal, rank-1, and full-rank covariance for two distinct samples of an N=20N=20 dataset (different rows) from the synthetic data process defined above. We use R=1,024R=1{,}024. We report the closed-form ELBO for each approximate posterior and set of hyperparameters (using Eq. 5) and the closed-form log-marginal likelihood (LML) for each set of hyperparameters (using Eq. 4).

Using a diagonal covariance (left column), we observe clear underfitting. Here, hyperparameters like observation noise compensate for the underestimated approximate posterior variance forced by the zero-forcing property of the reverse Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence. Using a rank-1 covariance (middle column), we observe clear overfitting with σy→0\sigma_{y}\rightarrow 0, as predicted by our analysis. Reassuringly, using a full-rank covariance (right column), we observe good fits without degenerate hyperparameters. Surprisingly, among only the underfit and overfit version, Bayesian model selection via the exact LML sometimes prefers the overfit option, while the ELBO does not.

Fig. 2 shows the ELBO and LML using a diagonal, rank-1, and full-rank covariance as a function of the chosen number of parameters RR, while keeping N=20N=20.

6 DISCUSSION

Is the prior or likelihood misspecified? Overfitting in Bayesian models can occur when the likelihood is narrow and the prior is broad (Takada, 2018). However, the observed overfitting in our example is not a result of a misspecified prior or likelihood. The marginal likelihood in Eq. (4) is the exact same marginal likelihood as the Gaussian process regression model with a RBF kernel, where we have latent function values f∼𝒩⁡(0N,K)f\sim\mathcal{N}(0_{N},K) and then observed targets y|f∼𝒩⁡(f,σy2​IN)y\mid f\sim\mathcal{N}(f,\sigma_{y}^{2}I_{N}), as long as the approximation K≈Φ​Φ⊤K\approx\Phi\Phi^{\top} is accurate. Instead, the observed overfitting results from the inability of the rank-1 covariance to match the true posterior.

Does empirical Bayes prevent the rank-1 covariance from overfitting? Empirical Bayes (EB) prevents overfitting by maximizing the LML, or the ELBO in VI, with respect to prior hyperparameters such as the prior variance τ\tau in p⁡(w)=𝒩⁡(w∣0R,τ​Σp)p(w)=\mathcal{N}(w\mid 0_{R},\tau\Sigma_{p}) (MacKay, 1992). For a rank-1 covariance, we find that EB regularizes the model by driving the prior variance toward the jitter value τ→ε\tau\rightarrow\varepsilon (phew, what a relief). Surprisingly, although the ELBO prefers this aggressive regularization, the LML does not (see Fig. 3).

Does tempered variational inference prevent overfitting? Tempered variational inference modifies the standard ELBO by scaling the expected log-likelihood by a factor of 1T\frac{1}{T}, where T>0T>0 denotes a temperature hyperparameter. Upweighting data in the ELBO has been shown to prevent underfitting for a Gaussian approximate posterior with an isotropic covariance (Harvey et al., 2024; Harvey et al., 2026). We show that downweighting data in the ELBO can prevent overfitting for a rank-1 covariance (see App. E).

Will tighter bounds prevent overfitting? Tighter bounds such as the importance weighted evidence lower bound (IWELBO; Burda et al., 2016) should in the infinite sample limit prevent underfitting for a Gaussian approximate posterior with a diagonal covariance. However, the convergence of the IWELBO to the LML relies on the absolute continuity of the approximate posterior. A rank-1 covariance without jitter is not absolutely continuous, since uncertainty is limited to a single direction. As a result, the IWELBO will not prevent overfitting in our example.

7 CONCLUSION

We showed that in variational inference the ELBO does not always give rise to Occam’s razor. This behavior is determined by the flexibility of your assumed approximate posterior to match the true posterior.

We hope this paper highlights the need for better marginal likelihood-based objectives that are not biased by the assumptions we need to make in order to scale to modern models. Promising directions include modified ELBO objectives based off your assumed approximate posterior (Harvey et al., 2024; Harvey et al., 2026), tighter bounds such as the IWELBO, and more flexible divergence measures that are mode seeking not mode covering such as Rényi’s α\alpha-divergence (Li and Turner, 2016).

∂J∂μq\displaystyle\frac{\partial J}{\partial\mu_{q}} =−1T​σy2​Φ⊤​(Φ​μq−y)−1τ​μq\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{T\sigma_{y}^{2}}\Phi^{\top}(\Phi\mu_{q}-y)-\frac{1}{\tau}\mu_{q} (14)

∂J∂σq,r2\displaystyle\frac{\partial J}{\partial\sigma_{q,r}^{2}} =−12​(1T​σy2​‖ϕr‖22+1τ−1σq,r2)\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{T\sigma_{y}^{2}}\|\phi_{r}\|_{2}^{2}+\frac{1}{\tau}-\frac{1}{\sigma_{q,r}^{2}}\right) (16)
σq,r2∗\displaystyle\sigma_{q,r}^{2*} =11τ+1T​σy2​‖ϕr‖22\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\frac{1}{\tau}+\frac{1}{T\sigma_{y}^{2}}\|\phi_{r}\|_{2}^{2}} (17)
∂J∂σy2\displaystyle\frac{\partial J}{\partial\sigma_{y}^{2}} =−12​T​(Nσy2−1σy4​(‖y−Φ​μq‖22+∑r=1Rσq,r2​‖ϕr‖22))\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2T}\left(\frac{N}{\sigma_{y}^{2}}-\frac{1}{\sigma_{y}^{4}}\left(\|y-\Phi\mu_{q}\|_{2}^{2}+\sum_{r=1}^{R}\sigma_{q,r}^{2}\|\phi_{r}\|_{2}^{2}\right)\right) (18)
σy2∗\displaystyle\sigma_{y}^{2*} =1N​(‖y−Φ​μq‖22+∑r=1Rσq,r2​‖ϕr‖22)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\left(\|y-\Phi\mu_{q}\|_{2}^{2}+\sum_{r=1}^{R}\sigma_{q,r}^{2}\|\phi_{r}\|_{2}^{2}\right) (19)

C.2 Rank-1 Covariance

The closed-form ELBO for a Gaussian approximate posterior with a rank-1 covariance is

1T⋅𝔼q⁡(w)​[log⁡pη​(y∣w)]\displaystyle\frac{1}{T}\cdot\mathbb{E}_{q(w)}\left[\log p_{\eta}(y\mid w)\right] =−12​T​[N​log⁡(2​π​σy2)+1σy2​(‖y−Φ​μq‖22+vq⊤​Φ⊤​Φ​vq+ε​tr⁡(Φ​Φ⊤))]\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2T}\left[N\log(2\pi\sigma_{y}^{2})+\frac{1}{\sigma_{y}^{2}}\left(\|y-\Phi\mu_{q}\|_{2}^{2}+v_{q}^{\top}\Phi^{\top}\Phi v_{q}+\varepsilon\operatorname{tr}\left(\Phi\Phi^{\top}\right)\right)\right] (20)
−DKL(q(w)∥pη(w))\displaystyle-D_{\text{KL}}\left(q(w)\parallel p_{\eta}(w)\right) =−12​[1τ​(‖vq‖22+R​ε)+1τ​‖μq‖22−R+R​log⁡τ−(R−1)​log⁡ε−log⁡(‖vq‖22+ε)].\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{1}{\tau}\left(\|v_{q}\|_{2}^{2}+R\varepsilon\right)+\frac{1}{\tau}\|\mu_{q}\|_{2}^{2}-R+R\log\tau-(R-1)\log\varepsilon-\log\left(\|v_{q}\|_{2}^{2}+\varepsilon\right)\right]. (21)
∂J∂μq\displaystyle\frac{\partial J}{\partial\mu_{q}} =−1T​σy2​Φ⊤​(Φ​μq−y)−1τ​μq\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{T\sigma_{y}^{2}}\Phi^{\top}(\Phi\mu_{q}-y)-\frac{1}{\tau}\mu_{q} (22)
μq∗\displaystyle\mu_{q}^{*} =(1T​σy2​Φ⊤​Φ+1τ​IR)−1​1T​σy2​Φ⊤​y\displaystyle=\left(\frac{1}{T\sigma_{y}^{2}}\Phi^{\top}\Phi+\frac{1}{\tau}I_{R}\right)^{-1}\frac{1}{T\sigma_{y}^{2}}\Phi^{\top}y (23)
∂J∂σy2\displaystyle\frac{\partial J}{\partial\sigma_{y}^{2}} =−12​T​(Nσy2−1σy4​(‖y−Φ​μq‖22+vq⊤​Φ⊤​Φ​vq+ε​tr⁡(Φ​Φ⊤)))\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2T}\left(\frac{N}{\sigma_{y}^{2}}-\frac{1}{\sigma_{y}^{4}}\left(\|y-\Phi\mu_{q}\|_{2}^{2}+v_{q}^{\top}\Phi^{\top}\Phi v_{q}+\varepsilon\operatorname{tr}\left(\Phi\Phi^{\top}\right)\right)\right) (24)
σy2∗\displaystyle\sigma_{y}^{2*} =1N​(‖y−Φ​μq‖22+vq⊤​Φ⊤​Φ​vq+ε​tr⁡(Φ​Φ⊤))\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\left(\|y-\Phi\mu_{q}\|_{2}^{2}+v_{q}^{\top}\Phi^{\top}\Phi v_{q}+\varepsilon\operatorname{tr}\left(\Phi\Phi^{\top}\right)\right) (25)

C.3 Full-Rank Covariance

The closed-form ELBO for a Gaussian approximate posterior with a full-rank covariance is

1T⋅𝔼q⁡(w)​[log⁡pη​(y∣w)]\displaystyle\frac{1}{T}\cdot\mathbb{E}_{q(w)}\left[\log p_{\eta}(y\mid w)\right] =−12​T​[N​log⁡(2​π​σy2)+1σy2​‖y−Φ​μq‖22+1σy2​tr⁡(Φ​Σq​Φ⊤)]\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2T}\left[N\log(2\pi\sigma_{y}^{2})+\frac{1}{\sigma_{y}^{2}}\|y-\Phi\mu_{q}\|_{2}^{2}+\frac{1}{\sigma_{y}^{2}}\operatorname{tr}(\Phi\Sigma_{q}\Phi^{\top})\right] (26)
−DKL(q(w)∥pη(w))\displaystyle-D_{\text{KL}}\left(q(w)\parallel p_{\eta}(w)\right) =−12​[1τ​tr⁡(Σq)+1τ​‖μq‖22−R+R​log⁡τ−log⁡det⁡(Σq)].\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{1}{\tau}\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma_{q})+\frac{1}{\tau}\|\mu_{q}\|_{2}^{2}-R+R\log\tau-\log\operatorname{det}(\Sigma_{q})\right]. (27)
∂J∂μq\displaystyle\frac{\partial J}{\partial\mu_{q}} =−1T​σy2​Φ⊤​(Φ​μq−y)−1τ​μq\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{T\sigma_{y}^{2}}\Phi^{\top}(\Phi\mu_{q}-y)-\frac{1}{\tau}\mu_{q} (28)
μq∗\displaystyle\mu_{q}^{*} =(1T​σy2​Φ⊤​Φ+1τ​IR)−1​1T​σy2​Φ⊤​y\displaystyle=\left(\frac{1}{T\sigma_{y}^{2}}\Phi^{\top}\Phi+\frac{1}{\tau}I_{R}\right)^{-1}\frac{1}{T\sigma_{y}^{2}}\Phi^{\top}y (29)
∂J∂Σq\displaystyle\frac{\partial J}{\partial\Sigma_{q}} =−12​(1T​σy2​Φ⊤​Φ+1τ​IR)+12​Σq−1\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{T\sigma_{y}^{2}}\Phi^{\top}\Phi+\frac{1}{\tau}I_{R}\right)+\frac{1}{2}\Sigma_{q}^{-1} (30)
Σq∗\displaystyle\Sigma_{q}^{*} =(1T​σy2​Φ⊤​Φ+1τ​IR)−1\displaystyle=\left(\frac{1}{T\sigma_{y}^{2}}\Phi^{\top}\Phi+\frac{1}{\tau}I_{R}\right)^{-1} (31)
∂J∂σy2\displaystyle\frac{\partial J}{\partial\sigma_{y}^{2}} =−12​T​(Nσy2−1σy4​(‖y−Φ​μq‖22+tr⁡(Φ​Σq​Φ⊤)))\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2T}\left(\frac{N}{\sigma_{y}^{2}}-\frac{1}{\sigma_{y}^{4}}\left(\|y-\Phi\mu_{q}\|_{2}^{2}+\operatorname{tr}(\Phi\Sigma_{q}\Phi^{\top})\right)\right) (32)
σy2∗\displaystyle\sigma_{y}^{2*} =1N​(‖y−Φ​μq‖22+tr⁡(Φ​Σq​Φ⊤))\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\left(\|y-\Phi\mu_{q}\|_{2}^{2}+\operatorname{tr}(\Phi\Sigma_{q}\Phi^{\top})\right) (33)
